sections.title: Mission · Find System Data
paragraphs: Linux places different information in different parts of the system. Recognize where it stores or exposes configuration, processes, memory, messages, logs, devices, kernel information, and boot files.
bullets: ps, top, free, syslog, and dmesg

sections.title: Linux Uses a Filesystem Hierarchy
paragraphs: Linux organizes system data in a single directory tree rooted at /. Standard directories have recognizable roles, so the path often tells you the kind of data inside.

sections.title: /etc/
paragraphs: /etc/ commonly stores system-wide configuration files for the operating system and installed services.

sections.title: /var/log/
paragraphs: /var/log/ commonly stores system and application log files that record events over time.

sections.title: /boot/
paragraphs: /boot/ contains files needed during system startup, such as bootloader and kernel-related boot files.

sections.title: /dev/
paragraphs: /dev/ contains special device files representing hardware and virtual devices.

sections.title: /proc/
paragraphs: /proc/ is a virtual filesystem exposing process and running-kernel information rather than ordinary persistent files.

sections.title: Process Information in /proc
paragraphs: Running processes have numeric process IDs, and corresponding /proc/PID paths expose runtime information about them.

sections.title: /sys/
paragraphs: /sys/ is a virtual filesystem presenting kernel, device, driver, and other system information.

sections.title: Processes
paragraphs: A process is a running instance of a program. Linux tracks processes with process IDs and exposes information through tools and virtual filesystems.

sections.title: ps
paragraphs: ps displays a snapshot of processes at the moment the command runs.

sections.title: top
paragraphs: top provides a live, updating view of processes and resource use.

table.caption: Static versus live
rows: Live updating process and resource view

sections.title: free
paragraphs: free reports system memory usage and availability.

sections.title: Memory Addresses and Runtime Information
paragraphs: Memory and runtime information describes the active state of the system. Tools such as free and virtual filesystems such as /proc/ expose that changing state.

sections.title: System Messaging
paragraphs: Linux components produce messages about services, processes, devices, drivers, and the kernel. Those messages help administrators understand system events and failures.

sections.title: syslog
paragraphs: syslog refers to the system-logging mechanism used to collect and route messages.

sections.title: dmesg
paragraphs: dmesg displays messages from the kernel ring buffer, often useful for startup, hardware, and driver events.

sections.title: Exam Trap · syslog vs. dmesg
paragraphs: syslog is general system logging. dmesg focuses on kernel messages, including hardware and driver information.

sections.title: Logs Are Troubleshooting Evidence
paragraphs: Logs preserve evidence of what happened, when it happened, and which component reported it. Administrators correlate logs and live tools when diagnosing a problem.
